title: Primary immunodeficiencies
covers: Inborn errors of immunity: warning signs, classification, the main combined and antibody deficiencies with their genes, chronic granulomatous disease, and treatment options.

items.p: Primary immunodeficiencies (inborn errors of immunity) are genetic disorders of immune development or function. Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired: drugs, cancer, malnutrition, HIV.
Together they affect at least 1 in 1000 to 1 in 5000 people. The 2024 classification lists 559 entities in 10 groups.

Patients get recurrent or opportunistic infections. Many also show failure to thrive, allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoinflammation or autoimmunity. Immune deficiency and autoimmunity often occur together.

ul: Four or more new ear infections in a year
Two or more serious sinus infections or pneumonias in a year
Two or more months of antibiotics with little effect
Failure to gain weight; persistent thrush; recurrent deep abscesses
Need for intravenous antibiotics; deep-seated infections

items.p: Diagnosis: history, flow cytometry, immunoglobulin levels, genetic testing. Earlier diagnosis means better survival.
The T-cell defect harms both cellular and antibody immunity. Babies look well at birth, then develop opportunistic infections.
Never give live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products. Cure is by stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy.
SCID means very low T cells. Subtypes are named by which cells remain.
The γ chain is shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21.
ADA deficiency: first PID gene defect described; high adenosine and deoxyadenosine. Treat with matched transplant, PEG-ADA enzyme replacement or gene therapy.
Omenn syndrome: partial (hypomorphic) RAG defect. Red, peeling skin, eosinophilia, large nodes, liver and spleen.

summary.h: Combined deficiencies with T cells present

ul: Hyper-IgM syndrome: CD40L (X-linked) or CD40 (autosomal recessive). T and B cells cannot cooperate. IgM normal or high; IgG, IgA and IgE very low; no germinal centers.
MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome II): mutated transcription factors such as CIITA. CD4 cells and antibody responses fail, but the T-cell count is normal.

items.p: Cellular immunity is normal. Symptoms begin after 6 months, when maternal IgG fades.
Typical infections: sinuses, ears and lungs, with pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and Staphylococcus aureus. Treatment is immunoglobulin replacement.

ul: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton): BTK mutation. Pre-B cells cannot mature. No B cells, no plasma cells, no immunoglobulin.
Common variable immunodeficiency: B cells present, low switched antibodies. Mostly sporadic, cause usually unknown; about 20% have autoimmunity.
Chronic granulomatous disease: defective NADPH oxidase, so no respiratory burst. Diagnosed with the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow test: normal neutrophils turn DHR fluorescent, patient cells do not.
Familial Mediterranean fever: MEFV gene, pyrin protein, overactive inflammasome.
Stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy: SCID and CID
Thymus transplantation: FOXN1 deficiency, DiGeorge syndrome
Small molecules such as JAK inhibitors: selected dysregulation disorders

cards.a: Primary: genetic. Secondary: acquired (immunosuppressive drugs, cancer, malnutrition, HIV).

cards.q: Most severe and most common groups of PID
cards.a: Most severe: combined immunodeficiencies. Most common: antibody deficiencies (about 50%).

cards.q: Two things never to give a child with SCID or CID
cards.a: Live virus vaccines and non-irradiated blood products

cards.q: What defines SCID among combined immunodeficiencies?
cards.a: T-cell lymphopenia
T− B− NK+ SCID; autosomal recessive (V(D)J recombination fails)
γ chain (IL2RG) deficiency: X-linked, T− B+ NK−

cards.q: Which receptors share the common γ chain?

cards.a: T− B− NK− SCID, autosomal recessive; toxic purine metabolites (adenosine, deoxyadenosine)
HLA-identical transplant (first choice), PEG-ADA enzyme replacement, gene therapy
Hypomorphic RAG mutations: erythroderma, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, infections
CD40L (X-linked, type 1) or CD40 (autosomal recessive, type 3)
Normal or high IgM; very low IgG, IgA, IgE; normal B-cell count; no germinal centers
No MHC class II expression (transcription factor genes such as CIITA); CD4 and antibody defects with a normal T-cell count

cards.q: Why do antibody deficiencies appear after 6 months of age?
cards.a: Maternal IgG transferred across the placenta declines.
Sinopulmonary infections and otitis with extracellular bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae, S. aureus)
BTK; pre-B cells cannot mature, so no B cells, plasma cells or immunoglobulin
B cells present but poor antibody production; mostly sporadic; about 20% autoimmunity; treated with immunoglobulin

cards.q: Chronic granulomatous disease: defect and test
cards.a: NADPH oxidase; dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry

cards.q: Familial Mediterranean fever: gene and protein
cards.a: MEFV; pyrin (overactive inflammasome)
Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy, as early as possible
Partial, not complete, loss of gene function

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a cause of secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Secondary immunodeficiencies are acquired (immunosuppressive treatment, cancer, malnutrition, viral infection such as HIV). Primary immunodeficiencies are genetic. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: How are inborn errors of immunity defined, and what is their estimated collective prevalence today?

options.A: Rare genetic disorders of immune development or function; 1/10,000 to 1/50,000
options.B: Acquired disorders of immune function after infection; at least 1/1000 to 1/5000
options.C: Common polygenic disorders of antibody production; about 1/100
options.D: Rare genetic disorders of immune development or function; at least 1/1000 to 1/5000
options.E: Rare genetic disorders limited to T cells; about 1/1,000,000

questions.explanation: Inborn errors of immunity (PIDs) are a heterogeneous group of rare genetic disorders affecting development and/or function of the immune system. Traditional estimate: 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 50,000 births; collective prevalence now at least 1/1000–1/5000. A: That is the traditional estimate. B: They are genetic. C: Not the definition or figure given. E: They form a heterogeneous group, and the figure is wrong.

questions.stem: Besides recurrent or opportunistic infections, which non-infectious manifestations may PID patients show?

options.A: Failure to thrive, obesity, lymphopenia in each case, and hypertension
options.B: Failure to thrive, allergy, lymphoproliferation or autoimmunity
options.C: Tall stature, allergy and resistance to autoimmunity
options.E: Autoinflammation, deafness in each case, and renal stones

questions.explanation: Non-infectious manifestations: failure to thrive, allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoinflammation and/or autoimmunity. Some forms are syndromic. A: Not the list given. C: Autoimmunity is a manifestation, not something patients resist. D: Not the list given. E: Not the list given.

questions.stem: According to the Jeffrey Modell Foundation's ten warning signs, which finding should raise suspicion of a PID?

options.A: Two new ear infections within one year
options.C: Two weeks on antibiotics with good effect
options.D: One sinus infection within one year
options.E: Four or more new ear infections within one year

questions.explanation: Ten warning signs include: four or more new ear infections in a year, two or more serious sinus infections, two or more months on antibiotics with little effect, two or more pneumonias in a year, failure to gain weight, recurrent deep abscesses, persistent thrush, need for IV antibiotics, two or more deep-seated infections, family history. A: The threshold for children is four or more. B: The sign is two or more pneumonias within a year. C: The sign is two or more months on antibiotics with little effect. D: The sign is two or more serious sinus infections within a year.

questions.stem: What is the "new paradigm" of PIDs adopted since the mid 2010s?

options.A: Immunodeficiency and autoimmunity are opposite, mutually exclusive states
options.B: PIDs are infections of the immune system by opportunistic organisms
options.C: Dysregulation gives both infection susceptibility and autoimmunity
options.D: Autoimmunity protects PID patients from infection
options.E: PIDs are limited to antibody deficiency

questions.explanation: Old paradigm: underactive system = immunodeficiency, overactive = autoimmunity. New paradigm: the two overlap; dysregulation of immune function often produces increased susceptibility to infection as well as autoimmunity/autoinflammation. A: That is the old paradigm. B: They are genetic disorders. D: Not the paradigm. E: The field covers many categories.

questions.stem: Which entity is paired with the year shown on the lecture's timeline?
questions.explanation: Timeline: SCID 1950, XLA 1952, CGD 1954, X-linked hyper-IgM 1961, ADA SCID molecular basis 1972. A: 1972 is the molecular basis of ADA SCID. C: CGD is dated 1954. D: SCID is dated 1950. E: It is dated 1961.

questions.stem: Which set contains "new warning signs" beyond infection?

options.A: Autoimmune cytopenia, unusual pathogens and endocrinopathy
options.C: Restricted pathogen pattern and cancer predisposition

questions.explanation: New warning signs: autoimmune cytopenia, lymphoproliferation, cancer predisposition, eczema/erythroderma, endocrinopathy, enteropathy/IBD, systemic autoimmunity/vasculitis. A: Unusual pathogens belong to the classical infectious signs. B: Severe infections are classical signs. C: The first is a classical infectious sign. E: Recurrent infections are classical signs.

questions.stem: How many PID entities does the IUIS 2024 classification recognize, and in how many tables?
questions.explanation: IUIS 2024 (published April 2025): 559 different PID entities in 10 tables/categories sharing similar phenotypes or molecular bases. B: There are 10 categories. C: The number is 559. D: Not the figures given. E: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: Which group of primary immunodeficiencies is the most common?
questions.explanation: IUIS 2024 lists 559 PIDs in 10 categories; combined immunodeficiencies are the most severe and antibody deficiencies the most common (about 50%). A: The most severe. B: Less common. C: Less common. D: Less common.

questions.stem: In a child with suspected primary immunodeficiency, which test counts the lymphocyte subsets?
questions.explanation: Diagnosis rests on history, flow cytometry, Ig levels and genetic testing; it guides therapy (IVIG, HSCT, gene therapy, prophylaxis, small molecules). A: Measures antibody, not cells. B: Finds the mutation. D: Not the test given. E: Not a diagnostic test for PID.

questions.stem: In the transplantation data shown, which children had the lowest survival (50%)?

options.A: Those younger than 3.5 months without infection at transplantation
options.B: Those older than 3.5 months with active infection at transplantation
options.C: Those older than 3.5 years with no infection
options.D: Those transplanted in the first month of life
options.E: Those younger than 3.5 months with resolved infection

questions.explanation: Age at transplantation and infection status significantly affect survival; it was lowest (50%) in children older than 3.5 months with active infection at the time of transplantation. A: Early transplantation without infection gives the best survival. C: The cut-off is 3.5 months, with active infection. D: Early is better. E: Not the lowest group.

questions.stem: A newborn with severe combined immunodeficiency looks healthy at birth. What appears over the following months?
questions.explanation: CID/SCID: defective T cell development or function impairs both cellular and humoral immunity; patients are asymptomatic at birth, then develop opportunistic infections. A: Autoinflammatory disease. B: CGD. D: Antibody deficiency, later. E: Not SCID.

questions.stem: An infant with suspected SCID needs a platelet transfusion and is due for routine immunization. Which precautions are needed?

options.A: Avoid inactivated vaccines and irradiated blood products
options.B: Give live vaccines early to stimulate T cells
options.C: Avoid IVIG and antibiotics before transplantation
options.D: Give non-irradiated platelets to supply donor lymphocytes
options.E: Avoid live virus vaccines and non-irradiated blood products

questions.explanation: Live virus vaccines and non-irradiated blood or platelet transfusions are dangerous in CID. A: The danger is with live vaccines and non-irradiated products. B: Live vaccines are dangerous. C: Not stated. D: Non-irradiated products are dangerous.

questions.stem: What distinguishes SCID within the combined immunodeficiencies?

options.A: B-cell lymphopenia with normal T cells
options.B: Normal T-cell numbers with impaired function
options.C: Absent NK cells in each subtype

questions.explanation: Both CID and SCID are defects of adaptive immunity, but SCID forms are characterized by T-cell lymphopenia. Subtypes are B+/B− and NK+/NK−. A: SCID is defined by low T-cell numbers. B: That describes CID with residual T cells. C: NK cells may be present or absent. E: Not SCID.

questions.stem: Which interventions are curative for SCID and CID?
questions.explanation: Curative interventions are HSCT and gene therapy, both with a high risk of morbidity and mortality; early diagnosis allows treatment at a young age and raises survival. B: Supportive, not curative. C: Thymus transplantation is for FOXN1 deficiency and DiGeorge syndrome. D: PEG-ADA applies to ADA deficiency. E: Live vaccines are dangerous.

questions.stem: An infant with SCID has no T cells but normal numbers of B cells and NK cells. Which defect fits this pattern?
questions.explanation: SCID arises from four mechanisms: rearrangement machinery (RAG: T−B−NK+), cytokine signaling (γ chain, JAK3: T−B+NK−), CD3 genes (T−B+NK+) and lymphocyte survival (ADA: T−B−NK−). A: T−B−NK+. B: T−B+NK−. D: T−B−NK−. E: B cells absent, T cells normal.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old has severe fungal, viral and bacterial infections, rash and chronic diarrhea. T and B cells are absent; NK cells are present. Which defect of the V(D)J rearrangement machinery fits?
questions.explanation: RAG1/RAG2 deficiency (chr. 11p12, autosomal recessive) impairs V(D)J rearrangement: T−B−NK+ SCID with onset at 2–3 months; susceptibility to opportunistic pathogens or live-vaccine organisms is pathognomonic. A: That gives T−B+NK− SCID. C: That gives T−B−NK− SCID. D: That gives T−B+NK+ SCID. E: That gives absent B cells with normal T cells.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has T−B+NK− SCID; his mother's brother died of infections in infancy. Which gene is most likely mutated?
questions.explanation: γ chain deficiency: IL2RG on Xq13; X-linked recessive T−B+NK− SCID; the most common SCID except in consanguineous populations (JAK3 deficiency uses the same pathway). A: T−B−NK+, autosomal recessive. B: T−B−NK−, autosomal recessive. C: T−B+NK+. D: B cells absent, T cells normal.

questions.stem: The common γ chain is part of the receptor for which cytokine?
questions.explanation: The γ chain is shared by the IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21 receptors. A: Not a γ-chain receptor. B: Not a γ-chain receptor. C: Not a γ-chain receptor. E: Not a γ-chain receptor.

questions.stem: Which SCID phenotype results from defects in the genes encoding the CD3 molecules?
questions.explanation: CD3 gene defects give T−B+NK+ SCID. B: RAG deficiency. C: γ chain deficiency. D: ADA deficiency. E: Not a SCID phenotype given.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old has T−B−NK− SCID with raised blood deoxyadenosine. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: ADA deficiency: first genetic defect described in PID; ADA on 20q13; AR T−B−NK− SCID; onset in the first month in 85–90%; raised adenosine and 2′-deoxyadenosine. A: NK cells present. B: B cells only. D: CGD. E: T−B+NK−.

questions.stem: Which laboratory findings are listed for ADA deficiency?

options.A: Hypergammaglobulinemia, normal CD4/CD8 ratio, low adenosine and 2'-deoxyadenosine
options.B: Normal or increased IgM with deficient IgG, IgA and IgE
options.C: Absent B cells with normal pre-B cells in marrow
options.D: Eosinophilia with elevated IgE and erythroderma

questions.explanation: Labs: hypogammaglobulinemia, reversed CD4+/CD8+ ratio, elevated serum adenosine and 2'-deoxyadenosine. A: The opposite pattern. B: That is hyper-IgM syndrome. C: That is XLA. D: That suggests Omenn syndrome.

questions.stem: What is the treatment of choice for ADA-deficient SCID?
questions.explanation: ADA-SCID: HLA-identical BMT is the treatment of choice; enzyme replacement with weekly PEG-ADA and gene therapy are alternatives. A: An alternative. B: An alternative. C: Not curative. E: FOXN1, DiGeorge.

questions.stem: How do CIDs differ mechanistically from SCIDs in the lecture?

options.A: Defects in early T-cell development leave no T cells
options.B: Residual T cells with impaired function
options.C: Defects in B-cell maturation leave T cells intact
options.D: Defects in phagocyte killing leave lymphocytes intact
options.E: Defects in complement leave adaptive immunity intact

questions.explanation: CID: defects altering the later stages in T-cell development or signaling give residual T cells with impaired function. A: That describes SCID. C: That describes antibody deficiency. D: That describes CGD. E: Not CID.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent infections with a normal B cell count, high IgM and very low IgG, IgA and IgE; his maternal uncle had the same disease. Lymph nodes lack germinal centers. Which molecule is defective?
questions.explanation: CD40L deficiency (Xq26): X-linked hyper-IgM type 1; defective T–B cooperation, no germinal centers, no isotype switching. CD40 deficiency is AR (type 3). B: Autosomal recessive hyper-IgM type 3. C: No B cells. D: Bare lymphocyte syndrome. E: CGD.

questions.stem: Which statement about MHC class II deficiency is correct?

options.A: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II: mutations in the HLA-DR structural genes; X-linked SCID
options.B: Hyper-IgM syndrome type 3: mutations in CD40; autosomal recessive CID
options.C: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II: mutations in TAP; defective CD8 cells with normal antibodies
options.D: Omenn syndrome: hypomorphic RAG mutations; autosomal recessive
options.E: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II: CIITA-type transcription factor mutations; AR CID

questions.explanation: MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome II): genes CIITA, RFXANK, RFX5, RFXAP encode transcription factors regulating MHC II expression; AR CID with defective antigen presentation, defective activation and development of CD4+ cells and defective antibody production. A: The genes encode transcription factors, and inheritance is AR. B: A different entity. C: The defect is in MHC II expression, affecting CD4 cells and antibody production. D: A different entity.

questions.stem: An infant with combined immunodeficiency has a normal total CD3 T cell count, and his T cells proliferate normally to PHA, but CD4 help is lacking. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MHC II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome II; CIITA, RFXANK, RFX5, RFXAP): defective antigen presentation and CD4 development; unlike SCID, total CD3 count is normal and T cells respond to PHA. A: T cells absent. B: T cells absent. D: T cells absent. E: B cell defect.

questions.stem: What is preserved in predominantly antibody deficiencies?
questions.explanation: Antibody deficiencies: defective production of IgG, IgA, IgM or high-affinity antibody, with normal cellular immunity. A: Defective. C: Can be defective. D: Can be defective. E: Often impaired.

questions.stem: A boy was well until 7 months of age and then developed recurrent otitis media and pneumonia. Why do antibody deficiencies present at this age?

options.A: Maternal IgA in breast milk declines after 6 months
options.C: Live vaccines are first given after 6 months
options.D: Transplacental maternal IgG declines after 6 months
options.E: B cells first leave the marrow after 6 months

questions.explanation: Clinical manifestations start after the age of 6 months, when transplacentally derived maternal IgG levels decline. A: The reason given is decline of transplacental IgG. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with X-linked agammaglobulinemia has another severe infection. Which organism is typical?
questions.explanation: Antibody deficiencies: extracellular bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. aureus); recurrent sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, conjunctivitis. B: T cell defects. C: Phagocyte defects. D: T cell defects. E: T cell defects.

questions.stem: About what share of primary immunodeficiencies are antibody deficiencies?
questions.explanation: Antibody deficiencies are the most common PIDs, about 50% (WHO); treatment is immunoglobulin replacement and supportive care. A: About 50%. B: About 50%. C: About 50%. E: About 50%.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a molecular basis of antibody deficiency EXCEPT:

options.B: Defective activation of B cells by T cells
options.C: Defective NADPH oxidase in B cells
options.D: Inability to secrete Ig or defects in class switching

questions.explanation: Bases: absence of B cells; defect in activation of B cells by T cells or absence of T helper cells; inability to secrete Igs or class-switch defects; over-activation of suppressive T cells. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: An adult has recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia, low IgG and IgA, and B cells at 5% of lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Absent B cells: XLA and AR forms (BLNK, μ heavy chain); B cells > 1%: CVID. B: B cells absent. C: Infancy, T cells absent. D: Phagocyte defect. E: Combined defect in infancy.

questions.stem: A boy has no circulating B cells and no plasma cells, but normal pre-B cells in his marrow. Which gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: XLA (Bruton): BTK gene (Xq21.3–22); X-linked recessive; no Ig, plasma cells or circulating B cells; normal pre-B cells (block in pre-B maturation). A: γ chain SCID. B: Hyper-IgM. C: T−B− SCID. D: FMF.

questions.stem: About what share of patients with CVID have an autoimmune condition?
questions.explanation: CVID: common, variable etiology; low switched isotypes, impaired specific antibody; mostly sporadic, familial forms often AD; ~20% have autoimmunity. A: About 20%. C: About 20%. D: About 20%. E: About 20%.

questions.stem: To what can immune dysregulation disorders be due?

options.A: Defective phagocytosis, defective complement or absent B cells
options.B: Excess tolerance, excess apoptosis or decreased signaling
options.D: Defective V(D)J recombination or ADA deficiency

questions.explanation: Immune dysregulation disorders lead to autoimmune manifestations as well as increased susceptibility to infection; they can be due to defective tolerance, defective apoptosis or increased cellular signaling. A: These define other PID groups. B: The opposite of what is listed. D: These cause SCID. E: Not genetic dysregulation.

questions.stem: What is the underlying defect in chronic granulomatous disease?

options.E: Defective BTK signaling in pre-B cells

questions.explanation: CGD is a primary immunodeficiency of phagocyte function due to defective NADPH oxidase (phox). B: The defect named is NADPH oxidase. C: That is ADA-SCID. D: That is FMF. E: That is XLA.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent abscesses. When his neutrophils are stimulated with PMA, they fail to convert dihydrorhodamine to fluorescent rhodamine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DHR assay: stimulated phagocytes make superoxide that reduces DHR to fluorescent rhodamine; no fluorescence = defective NADPH oxidase (CGD). A: B cell defect. B: T cell defect. C: Switching defect. D: Autoinflammatory.

questions.stem: Which categories make up the autoinflammatory diseases?

options.A: Periodic fever syndromes, antibody deficiencies and complement deficiencies
options.B: Type I interferonopathies, SCID and phagocyte defects
options.C: Sterile inflammation of joints, hyper-IgM and XLA
options.D: Periodic fever syndromes and type I interferonopathies
options.E: Periodic fever syndromes, CVID and bone marrow failure

questions.explanation: Autoinflammatory diseases: periodic fever syndromes, systemic inflammation with urticarial rash, sterile inflammation of the skin/bone/joints, type I interferonopathies. A: The latter are separate PID groups. B: The latter are separate groups. C: The latter are other entities. E: The latter are separate groups.

questions.stem: Which protein is encoded by the MEFV gene?
questions.explanation: Familial Mediterranean fever: MEFV (16p13.3) encodes pyrin; mutations increase inflammasome activation. A: Not MEFV. C: BTK. D: ADA. E: MHC II regulation.

questions.stem: For which conditions is thymus transplantation used?

options.A: ADA deficiency and γ chain deficiency

questions.explanation: Thymus transplantation is used in very few specific cases: FOXN1 deficiency and DiGeorge syndrome. A: These are treated by HSCT, gene therapy or enzyme replacement. B: These receive immunoglobulin replacement. C: Not treated by thymus transplantation. D: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about immunoglobulin replacement and CVID matches the lecture?

options.A: Immunoglobulin substitution cures CVID, so HSCT is not performed
options.B: Immunoglobulin substitution is contraindicated in XLA
options.C: HSCT is first-line in antibody deficiencies, with IVIG for 26% of failures
options.D: Ig substitution is standard, yet 26% of CVID patients undergo HSCT
options.E: Immunoglobulin substitution replaces HSCT in SCID

questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin substitution is adopted in patients with antibody deficiencies; 26% of patients with CVID still undergo HSCT. Patients with SCID and CID require HSCT. A: 26% still undergo HSCT. B: It is the treatment for antibody deficiencies. C: Reversed. E: SCID and CID require HSCT.

questions.stem: Which class of drugs is given as the example of targeted therapy with small molecules, and what guides the choice among them?

options.A: JAK inhibitors; patient age and blood group
options.C: JAK inhibitors; toxicity profile and disease

questions.explanation: Targeted therapies with small molecules: JAK inhibitors; the choice can be driven by the different toxicity profiles, availability of formulations and the disease to treat. A: Not the criteria listed. B: Not the example given. D: Not the example given. E: Not the example given.

questions.stem: What is a hypomorphic mutation?

options.A: One causing partial loss of gene function
options.B: One causing complete loss of gene function
options.C: One causing gain of a new function
options.E: One with no effect on the protein

questions.explanation: A hypomorphic mutation causes a partial loss of gene function (reduced expression or reduced functional performance, but not complete loss): one gene, different severities. B: That is a null (amorphic) mutation. C: Not hypomorphic. D: Not hypomorphic. E: Not hypomorphic.

questions.stem: An infant has desquamating erythroderma, recurrent pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Which genetic change is most likely?

options.A: Null mutations in the IL2RG gene

questions.explanation: Omenn syndrome: severe but incomplete T cell impairment, mostly hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 mutations (partial loss of function); AR. A: Classic γ chain SCID. C: ADA-SCID. D: XLA. E: FMF.

questions.stem: A girl has T−B+NK− SCID, but her IL2RG gene is normal. Which kinase in the same cytokine signaling pathway is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: JAK3 deficiency is discussed with γ chain deficiency: the γ chain signals through JAK3; both give T−B+NK− SCID (JAK3 is autosomal, so girls are affected). A: B cell signaling. B: Not discussed with the γ chain. C: Not discussed with the γ chain. E: Not the γ chain partner.
